title: A hymn in Bilaval
hookLine: Bilaval holds Guru Arjan's song of shelter from the hot wind, sung after the danger has passed

lines: A HYMN THAT SOUNDS LIKE IT.
cards: The storm blew all night. In the morning someone opens the front door and steps out to look: branches down, the street wet, the house still standing. Somebody puts the kettle on.
Somebody laughs at nothing. Somebody cries, and it isn't sad crying. Relief has a sound, and it's closer to joy than to quiet.
Today's hymn, in the raga opened yesterday, sounds like that doorway after the storm. Today: a hymn in Bilaval.

teach.b: First, the song. Bilaval holds hymns of Guru Arjan about shelter, and one of them, on ang eight nineteen, begins taatee vaao na lagaee: the hot wind doesn't touch the one in the refuge of the Supreme Lord.
Earlier on this path you opened its pictures: the scorching wind, the refuge, the protective line drawn on four sides. Today, listen for the tense. Second, the verbs.
In paraphrase: I met the perfect Guru, who arranged all this. He gave the medicine of the Lord's Name. The Protector protected me and erased every illness.
Grace came, says Nanak, and God became my helper.
Met, gave, protected, erased, came. Nearly all of it already happened. This isn't a plea shouted into the storm.
It's a song sung after the wind has dropped.

teach.h: A STORY OF A SON WHO RECOVERED.
teach.b: Third, the story people tell. Some Sikh tellers link Guru Arjan's Bilaval hymns of this kind to a time when his young son Hargobind fell ill and recovered.
The hymn names no one, so hold that as tradition, not as the text. Fourth, why a raga of joy. Shelter and joy are two halves of one moment.
Fear runs ahead of the danger; thanks runs behind it. Guru Arjan set that relief in Bilaval, the raga tradition links with morning joy, so the thanks would be sung, not just felt.

how: Guru Arjan's Bilaval shabad taatee vaao na lagaee is sung in kirtan and recited by Sikhs for protection and in thanks, at times of illness and recovery, before journeys and at births.

games.q: what does “a hymn in bilaval” mean?
o: a warning song about storms still to come
a plea for rain during the hot summer wind
Guru Arjan's thanks for shelter, sung after danger

games.q: inside the Bilaval hymn — tap the pairs.
p: mostly past: the danger has passed

s: the hymn is mostly a plea shouted during the danger
nearly all of it is told as already done: met, gave, protected, erased.
some tellers link it to his recovery, but the hymn names no one.
the hymn is in a raga linked with joy
it's in Bilaval, the joyful morning raga.

games.q: the hot wind has passed. the illness is gone. you're the singer. what do you do now?
o: move on quickly and try not to think about it.
sing the thanks out loud, in a joyful raga.
start worrying about the next storm.
games.why: Guru Arjan sings it: the Protector protected me, grace came, God became my helper, set in Bilaval, the raga of morning joy.

practice: Bring back one time something passed that you feared wouldn't, an illness, a bad night, a test result, and skip the fear: go straight to the moment after, when it was over.
Feel where the relief sits in the body now, the chest, the shoulders, the face, and stay there, with one Waheguru as thanks if you pray, or the relief as the whole of it if you don't.

wordCard.voice: A hymn in Bilaval. Guru Arjan's song of shelter from the hot wind, told mostly in the past tense: the danger passed, and the thanks is sung in a raga of joy. Today's word.

orig.note: taatee vaao, the hot wind of the Punjab summer, which the hymn says does not touch the one in the Lord's refuge.

carryVoice: Your line: joy and shelter. The hot wind passed, and the song came after. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bilaval Mahalla 5, Ang 819 (taatee vaao na lagaee paarbraham sarnaaee; the line on four sides; the perfect Guru; the medicine of the Name; the Protector erased every illness; Nanak: grace, God became my helper)
the young Hargobind's illness and recovery, linked by some tellers to Guru Arjan's Bilaval hymns
